entries.name: Paula of Rome
entries.statusDescription: Not counted as a candidate tradition of its own — its story is told plainly inside another tradition's, rather than standing alone.
entries.sourcing:
Thin for her own voice, rich for her life. Her own words survive in one letter, Letter 46, sent from Bethlehem in 386 in her name and her daughter Eustochium's. It urges their friend Marcella to join them. The Library's editor says Jerome wrote it for them. Nearly all else we know comes from Jerome's Letter 108, written soon after she died.

Jerome, who taught her, wrote the full account of her, and he wrote it to praise her.

One outside report survives in two forms. In the Greek Lausiac History, a monk says Paula, who looks after Jerome, will die first and be freed from his bad temper. A later Syriac version says she died before her time to escape his envy and evil-eyedness. Our sources do not settle which is right.
entries.floorNote: Her faith is not in question.
entries.relationsSummary: Told within the Hieronymian circle, with Jerome and her daughter Eustochium. She left Rome for the holy places. At Bethlehem she set up a monastery for men and put the women who joined her into three houses.
entries.why: Paula was a Roman noblewoman and a widow. She gave her goods to her children and sailed east with her daughter Eustochium. At Bethlehem she led a community of women and studied Scripture with Jerome.
entries.teaser: Rome and Bethlehem, c. 386 to 404 CE: a noblewoman who left her palace for a mud cabin, and learned Hebrew so she could chant the psalms in it.
entries.longDescription:
Paula came from a noble Roman family. Jerome says it traced its line to the Gracchi and the Scipios. She married Toxotius and bore five children, among them Eustochium, Rufina and a son, Toxotius. When her husband died, Jerome writes, her grief nearly killed her. She then gave herself to the service of the Lord.

Later she sailed east from Portus with Eustochium. On the shore her small son held out his hands, and Rufina begged her to wait until she was married. Jerome says her eyes stayed dry. She toured the holy places, then settled at Bethlehem and built cells and monastic buildings there.

She set up a monastery for men. She also gathered women from many provinces and divided them into three houses, which met for psalms and prayer. She read the Old and New Testaments under Jerome's guidance. She learned Hebrew well enough to chant the psalms in it. Jerome says she died after twenty years at Bethlehem, aged fifty-six.
voices: Paula of Rome — whose letter to Marcella, sent with her daughter, the Library holds among Jerome's letters
Jerome — her teacher, who wrote her epitaph in Letter 108
Eustochium — her daughter, who sailed with her and shared her vows
entries.legacy:
Later Catholic writers hold her up as a model. A Catholic Life of Lady Magdalen Montague, printed in English in 1627, cites Jerome on "the most noble widdow S. Paula" to show how its heroine mourned her husband.

In Mexico, the nun Sor Juana Ines de la Cruz calls her "my most holy Mother Paula" and names her as a woman learned in Hebrew, Greek and Latin. Sor Juana says that she, a nun and "daughter of a St. Jerome and of a Santa Paula", would fall short of such learned parents if she stayed ignorant.

entries.name: Constantine the Great
entries.statusDescription: Not counted as a candidate tradition of its own — its story is told plainly inside another tradition's, rather than standing alone.
entries.sourcing:
Rich, but through Eusebius. The Library holds the Edict of Milan and letters issued in Constantine's name. Eusebius copied them whole. He also records an Oration to the Assembly of the Saints, which he says Constantine wrote.

How and when he was baptized is disputed. Eusebius says Constantine asked the bishops for baptism near Nicomedia, close to the end of his life.

A Syriac chronicle that goes under Zachariah's name says Eusebius is wrong. It says the emperor was not baptized at the end of his life, and it points to the story of his conversion by Silvester at Rome.
entries.floorNote: Not in question. He called the bishops to the council at Nicaea.
entries.relationsSummary: Told within Imperial and Juridical Christianity. It opens in 312, when he first let the church worship freely. He called the bishops to Nicaea and wrote letters and edicts on church quarrels.
entries.why: Constantine was the Roman emperor who ended the ban on the church. With Licinius he gave Christians, and all others, freedom to follow the religion they chose. He called the bishops to a great council at Nicaea. He also judged church quarrels and moved against groups he called heretics.
entries.teaser: Milan and Nicaea, 312 to 337 CE: the emperor who let Christians worship, met their bishops at Nicaea, and sought baptism near his death.
entries.longDescription:
In 312 Constantine began to tolerate the church. Later he and Licinius met at Milan. Their edict gave Christians and all others the freedom to follow the religion they chose. Eusebius copies it whole.

A quarrel among African Christians, the Donatists, also came to him. He gave them judges, and the bishop of Rome sat with them. Donatus appealed. Constantine answered in the words Optatus gives: "Oh, mad daring of their fury!"

He called the bishops to Nicaea, says Eusebius. He wrote to Macarius of Jerusalem about a church at Christ's tomb. An edict of his takes away the houses of several groups, such as Novatians and Marcionites. Near Nicomedia he asked the bishops for baptism. He died there on 22 May 337.
voices: Constantine — emperor, whose edicts and letters the Library holds as Eusebius copied them
Eusebius of Caesarea — who copied his documents and wrote his Life
Optatus of Milevis — a Catholic bishop who tells how Constantine met the Donatist appeal
entries.legacy:
Syriac writers, far from Rome, still name him. Michael the Syrian was a Syriac Orthodox patriarch. He says a monk of Alexandria wrote "from Adam to the emperor Constantine".

A Syriac chronicle says Constantine and Helena built the church at Christ's tomb. The Persians took Jerusalem, and it burned.

The chronicle under Zachariah's name disputes Eusebius on his baptism. Eusebius has him ask for it near the end of his life. The chronicle says he was not baptized then, and it cites the story of his conversion by Silvester, kept in writing and in pictures at Rome.

entries.name: Basil of Caesarea
entries.statusDescription: Not counted as a candidate tradition of its own — its story is told plainly inside another tradition's, rather than standing alone.
entries.sourcing:
Rich. The Library holds his letters and his treatise On the Holy Spirit in English. It holds his Ascetic Works, with the Longer and Shorter Rules, and his Address to Young Men. It also holds his Hexaemeron homilies and his three books Against Eunomius in Greek and Latin.

Some famous works are disputed. Letter 38, often used to show that the three Cappadocians agreed, may be by Basil or by his brother Gregory of Nyssa.
entries.floorNote: His faith is not in question.
entries.relationsSummary: Told within the Cappadocians, with his brother Gregory of Nyssa and his friend Gregory of Nazianzus. He wrote On the Holy Spirit against those who ranked the Spirit below the Father and the Son. He made his brother and his friend bishops, and the friend resented it for years.
entries.why: Basil was bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia from about 370. His treatise On the Holy Spirit answered those who ranked the Spirit below the Father and the Son. He argued from how the church already prayed. A council in 787 told double monasteries to keep his rule, and later churches call him "the Great".
entries.teaser: Caesarea in Cappadocia, c. 329 to 379 CE: a bishop who defended the Spirit's place beside the Father and the Son, and wrote a rule for monks that a council and Benedict still named.
entries.longDescription:
Basil was born in 329 or 330 in Cappadocia. He writes that his grandmother Macrina, a woman of Neocaesarea, brought him up. She had kept the words of Gregory the Wonder-worker, and she shaped him in them as a child.

In 370 Eusebius of Caesarea died, and Basil was made bishop in his place. Anthimus of Tyana claimed rights over part of the province, and Basil resisted him. To strengthen his hand, Basil set up new bishoprics. He made his brother Gregory bishop of Nyssa and his friend Gregory bishop of Sasima. The friend took it ill.

Some bishops said the Spirit could not be ranked with the Father and the Son. Not long after 373, Basil answered them in On the Holy Spirit, written for Amphilochius. He argued from the church's own practice, such as its form of doxology. He says it comes down from Gregory the Wonder-worker, the old bishop of Neocaesarea. Basil died on 1 January 379.
voices: Basil of Caesarea — bishop, theologian and teacher of monks, whose letters and treatises the Library holds
Macrina the elder — his grandmother, known through his letter to the Neocaesareans
Gregory of Nazianzus — his friend, whom he made bishop of Sasima
entries.legacy:
Later churches call him "the Great". Mark of Ephesus cites what Basil the Great says in his own prayers, which were said each year at Pentecost. Dositheus and his synod at Jerusalem, in 1672, name "Basil the Great" too. They say he answered slander in one short letter.

The Second Council of Nicaea, in 787, told double monasteries to keep "the rule of our holy Father Basil". Benedict's Rule lists "the Rule of our Holy Father St. Basil" among the books for monks.

Gennadius says Rufinus put works of Basil into Latin.

Jerome says Ambrose's Six Days took more from Basil than from Origen.

entries.name: Gregory of Nazianzus
entries.statusDescription: Not counted as a candidate tradition of its own — its story is told plainly inside another tradition's, rather than standing alone.
entries.sourcing: Rich. The Library holds his Select Orations, his Select Letters and the Five Theological Orations in English. It holds his orations and letters in Greek and Latin, his two Invectives against Julian, and his poem on the books of Scripture.
entries.floorNote: His faith is not in question. Later churches call him "the Theologian", a title the editors say he shares with John the Evangelist alone among the Fathers.
entries.relationsSummary: Told within the Cappadocians, with his friend Basil. In 381 he took the chair of the great council, then resigned. He wrote two letters against Apollinarius.
entries.why: Gregory was a bishop, preacher and poet. He was born at Arianzus, near Nazianzus. His Five Theological Orations defend faith in the Trinity. They won him the title "the Theologian".
entries.teaser: Nazianzus and Constantinople, c. 372 to 390 CE: the preacher called the Theologian, who took the chair of the great council of 381, then resigned and went home.
entries.longDescription:
Gregory was born at Arianzus, a country estate near Nazianzus. Basil was his friend. About 372 Basil made him bishop of Sasima, a miserable little village. Gregory was angry, and the two were on strained terms for a long time.

Theodosius gave him the churches of Constantinople. In 381 the council made him bishop there. Its head, Meletius, died, and he took the chair. Egyptian bishops objected, and he resigned.

Gregory wrote two letters to the priest Cledonius against Apollinarius. In the first he writes that what Christ has not taken on, he has not healed. After the council Gregory went home to Nazianzus. He retired to Arianzus about the end of 383, and he died there in 389 or 390.
voices: Gregory of Nazianzus — bishop, preacher and poet, whose orations, letters and poems the Library holds
Basil of Caesarea — his friend, who made him bishop of Sasima
Cledonius — the priest to whom he wrote against Apollinarius
entries.legacy:
Both sides of the English quarrel of the 1500s quote him. John Jewel, for the Church of England, cites him on "the pitiful state of his own time", to show that Christians then also lived badly. The Catholic priest Robert Southwell cites him on life as a child's game, building houses of sand on the shore.

Jerome calls him "my instructor in the Scriptures". Gennadius says Rufinus put his works into Latin, as he did Basil's.

Paula: a census place entry for Bethlehem (placeId, pleiadesId) so modernCountries can name it. No existing entry carries Bethlehem; the entry uses Rome only, as the home tradition and Jerome's record do.

Constantine: the Library holds Michael the Syrian only to the Constantine hits listed in the count. If Mark wants the Syriac Orthodox claim of a different baptism story shown more fully, a text of the Chronicle of 1234 or of Zachariah's own book 1 Silvester narrative would help.
flags: Dates are life or working years from a source, each with a fact row. Paula: 386 is the date of Letter 46 written from Bethlehem; 404 is the date of her epitaph (Letter 108); the Library text gives her death by the consulship of Honorius and Aristaenetus, not by a year number, so end is the letter's date. Her birth year is not given. Basil: 329 or 330 (start 329); NPNF's own editor finds no reason to question 329 or 330. Gregory of Nazianzus: start 372 from Basil's chronology entry for 372; end 390 is the later of 'dying there in 389 or 390'. Constantine: start 312 rests on the census home record, not on a vendored text.

modernCountries: Paula uses Rome only (no Bethlehem entry exists; the home tradition and Jerome's census record do the same). Constantine copies the home tradition's Rome and Constantinople. Basil and Gregory of Nazianzus copy the Cappadocia entry of the home tradition and Gregory of Nyssa.
Ids checked against movements and retiredMovements: paula-of-rome, constantine-the-great, basil-of-caesarea and gregory-of-nazianzus are unused.

concerns, Paula: desert-monasticism--hieronymian-ascetic-literary names Paula but is about how the Hieronymian circle came to know Egyptian monasticism (Marcella hears of Antony and Pachomius from Athanasius; Jerome writes on Antony). Its three source quotes are Jerome's words, and only one is about Paula's act. concerns left null, not assigned to Paula; if one person takes it, it would be Jerome (already an entry; release 29 left it unset).

concerns assigned to constantine-the-great (null before): imperial-juridical-christianity--donatism, --montanism-the-new-prophecy, --novatianism--2, --jerusalem-liturgical-pilgrimage-christianity (each quotes his acts or words). Not assigned: palestinian-church-pre-constantinian--jerusalem-liturgical-pilgrimage-christianity (about continuity of the see; the Macarius letter is one of four sources), latin-apologists--imperial-juridical-christianity (about Lactantius), donatism--latin-pastoral-congregational-christianity--2 (about the origin of the schism), melitian-schism--cyrilline-miaphysite-egyptian-christianity and imperial-juridical-christianity--ebionite-nazoraean-current (about Eusebius and the Tyre synod). The other 'Constantine' links are namesakes (Constantine V, Constantine of Lampron, Constantinus the abbot, Cyril-Constantine).

concerns assigned to basil-of-caesarea: desert-monasticism--iconophile-byzantine-monasticism (Basil's own letter and the canon on his rule) and anatolian-church-third-century--cappadocian-nicene-pastoral-monastic-tradition (both sources are Basil's own words). Not assigned: desert-monasticism--early-benedictine-italian-monasticism (Benedict's Rule names Basil's Rule among others; it is about Benedict's reading) and gallic-monastic-ascetic-christianity--early-benedictine-italian-monasticism, desert-monasticism--insular-irish-monastic-christianity, byzantine and Bogomil links (namesakes).
concerns assigned to gregory-of-nazianzus: cappadocian-nicene-pastoral-monastic-tradition--apollinarian-christianity (all sources are his letters).

Link cappadocian-nicene-pastoral-monastic-tradition--aquileian-christianity names both Basil and Gregory of Nazianzus, but its sources quote Gennadius on Rufinus's work, not either man's words or acts. I left concerns null; if one person must take it, it would be neither, since the subject is Rufinus.

Links whose concerns are already set, and which name the new people (not overwritten): cappadocian-nicene-pastoral-monastic-tradition--pneumatomachian-current, --anomoean-eunomian-christianity, --imperial-juridical-christianity, homoian-arian-christianity--cappadocian-nicene-pastoral-monastic-tradition (all gregory-of-nyssa; also name Basil, and Gregory of Nazianzus in the last three); alexandria-catechetical--cappadocian-nicene-pastoral-monastic-tradition (origen; names Basil and Gregory of Nazianzus); alexandria-catechetical--ambrosian-milan-standalone (ambrose-of-milan; names Basil); cappadocian-nicene-pastoral-monastic-tradition--hieronymian-ascetic-literary (jerome; names Gregory of Nazianzus); hieronymian-ascetic-literary--jerusalem-liturgical-pilgrimage-christianity (jerome; names Paula); byzantine-imperial-church-justinianic--roman-church-gregorian and early-benedictine-italian-monasticism--roman-church-gregorian (gregory-the-great; they match Constantine only as a namesake or in passing).

Contested points tagged and given both sides: Paula's relation to Jerome (Greek Palladius: she will die first and be freed from his bad temper; Syriac version: she died before her time to escape his envy and evil-eyedness; entry does not choose); Constantine's baptism (Eusebius: near Nicomedia at the end of his life; Zachariah chronicle: not at the end of his life, conversion by Silvester at Rome). The Zachariah text is a composite work attributed to Pseudo-Zachariah; the entry says 'goes under Zachariah's name'.

Paula: the 1627 Montague Life is a badly garbled OCR scan and the Library marks it a second witness, not a quotable text. The fact-table quote keeps its garbled spelling ('widdow'); the entry quotes only that words. The Sor Juana fact rows quote the Library's OCR Spanish with its long-s misreadings ('doda' for 'docta', 'vná' for 'vna'). The Sor Juana line on being daughter of a St. Jerome and a Santa Paula uses the Opus-authored rendering from the review; the other two English lines were checked as sound in the review.

Constantine legacy: the Michael the Syrian line is a chronicle source-list note, the thinnest of the counted hits. The Library's OCR reads the chronicler as 'Anniajîus, moine d'Alexandrie'; I wrote 'a monk of Alexandria' and did not supply the name Annianus. I did not use Michael's line 16422 ('Constantine entered Rome; Sylvester and all Christians fled before him') because its context is unclear. The Chronica minora passage is placed on the Church of the East shelf by the census count, but the volume gathers East and West Syriac chroniclers, so the entry says only 'a Syriac chronicle'. It names the church 'aedes Resurrectionis (Anastasis)'; reading that as the church at Christ's tomb rests on Constantine's own letter to Macarius (Widely Accepted row).

Home record imperial-juridical-christianity is internally inconsistent on Constantine's toleration: its why field says 312, its longDescription says 313. The entry uses 312 (the people-row year and the why field) for start and for the opening line of longDescription.

Legacy sentences name later writers who 'name' or 'cite' the person; none says 'influenced', and no link is drafted. Basil's legacy goes beyond the two counted traditions (Benedict's Rule, Nicaea II, Gennadius on Rufinus, Jerome on Ambrose) because the census already cites each of those sources on an existing link; every one has a fact row.

Prose scoring and quote checks are run through check_draft.py; the sourcing lines on holdings for Basil's Address to Young Men and Gregory's Migne volumes and metrical poem rest on file names and the home people row, so those rows carry no quote.

Paula's own words: Letter 46 (Paula and Eustochium to Marcella), issued in her name, counts as her own words (ruling B, Decision-Log 2026-11-10, P2-G3b). The Library's editor says Jerome composed it; sourcing says so.

Gregory of Nazianzus's (the Theologian title) stays as a floor note about faith and doctrine; Constantine's baptism dispute moved to sourcing.
